newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian government gives ground on election row.
newsitem.headline: Serbian government gives ground on election row.

text.p: The Serbian government appeared to be giving in on Saturday to demands that opposition victories at disputed local elections be restored, agreeing with Belgrade students that November poll results must be respected.

"The Serbian government representatives agreed with the necessity that the will of the citizens expressed at local elections must be fully respected, underscoring that the government had clearly demanded this in its previous conclusions."
This was said a statement signed by Serbian deputy prime ministers Ratko Markovic and Nedeljko Sipovac and a delegation of student protesters in Belgrade.

"In keeping with this, the government will during the day order the Justice Ministry to demand of competent state bodies, which still have not finished establishing final election results, to do this as soon as possible," the statement said.

The opposition Zajedno coalition claimed it won in 14 of Serbia's 18 largest cities including the capital Belgrade and the second city, Nis, but Milosevic's Socialists annulled the victories, claiming unspecified irregularities.

The cancellation triggered a eight-week wave of daily street protests by Belgrade students and Zajedno supporters which became the most serious challenge to leftist rule in Serbia in the last 52 years.
Earlier this week the Serbian government ordered the election commission in Nis to concede the ruling (SPS) socialist party's election loss there.
"The competent state bodies will be demanded also to determine responsibility and adequate punishment in cases where election results were forged," the statement said.
The statement came hours after political sources had said Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic was expected to acknowledge opposition victories in the elections and call for a coalition government.
The students are demanding recognition of the Zajedno victories, free access to state media and the dismissal of Belgrade university's rector.
"Their stands and ours are identical on the three demands," Cedomir Jovanovic, a student protest leader, told Reuters.
"Markovic and Sipovac have scheduled a meeting for 1300 GMT with Justice Minister Arandjel Markicevic to tell him what they agreed with us."
"The talks were not unpleasant, they immediately expressed readiness to accept our demands," he said.
The Serbian government would meet after the responsible ministries had done their job, he said.
Jovanovic said the two ministers also agreed that the state television (RTS) coverage of the protests was bad.
"Markovic agreed that RTS news was counter-productive both for government and the ruling party."
Sources in Belgrade said Milosevic was preparing a major reshuffle in the government, the ruling party and state media after the election fiasco.
"It is definitely on, but will not happen until the crisis is over," a senior political source said.
"Markovic and Sipovac insisted particularly on the responsibility of those violating the law," Jovanovic said.
"Sipovac said much too much damage had been done to the reputation of both the country and the ruling party," Jovanovic said.
Sipovac said that the ruling socialists would win the coming republican elections, Jovanovic said.
"In order to do this, they will have to purge their ranks of those who turned a deaf ear to demands, and we were assured this would be so," he said.
Jovanovic said the two deputy prime ministers told the student delegation that the dismissal of the Belgrade University rector was imminent.
"We have no doubt that will not be so. We are of the impression they are not thrilled with rector's behaviour either and said that he, as an SPS member, had incurred a lot of damage," Jovanovic said.
